questions.prompt: Which command shows which files are modified, staged or untracked?
questions.explanation: git status summarises the working tree and staging area. git log shows history, push uploads commits, clone copies a repository.

questions.prompt: `git pull` is roughly `git fetch` followed by integrating the fetched changes (merge or rebase) into your current branch.
questions.explanation: fetch downloads remote commits; pull then integrates them into the current branch, by merge by default or by rebase if configured.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a feature branch for a new test?
options: It keeps your work isolated until it is reviewed and merged, so main stays stable
questions.explanation: Branches isolate work in progress. Main stays releasable, and the pull request lets others review the test before it lands.

questions.prompt: After these commands, what is the state of `config.properties`?
questions.code:
echo "browser=firefox" >> config.properties
git add config.properties
git status --short
questions.explanation: git add moves the change to the staging area; nothing was committed afterwards, so it is staged but not committed.

questions.prompt: You committed a password in `secrets.env` on your local branch but have not pushed. What is the right first step?
options: Push, then delete the file in a new commit
Remove it from the commit before pushing (for example `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, unstage, add it to .gitignore, recommit) and rotate the password if it might have leaked
questions.explanation: Once pushed, the secret lives in history even if deleted later. Fix the local commit before pushing and add the file to .gitignore. If there is any chance of exposure, rotate the credential.

questions.prompt: Which belong in a test project's .gitignore? Select all that apply.
options: Test reports and screenshots generated by runs
questions.explanation: Generated output and secrets should not be versioned. Test source code is exactly what should be committed.

questions.prompt: What does `git rebase main` do on your feature branch?
options: Replays your branch's commits on top of the latest main, rewriting their history
questions.explanation: Rebase moves your commits so they start from the tip of main, giving a linear history. Because it rewrites commits, avoid rebasing branches others have already pulled.

questions.prompt: A regression appeared somewhere in the last 64 commits and you have an automated test that detects it. Which approach finds the culprit fastest?
options: Check out each commit in order
Use `git bisect` (optionally `git bisect run <test command>`), which needs about 6 test runs
questions.explanation: Bisect is a binary search: log2(64) = 6 steps. With bisect run it is fully automated. Linear search can take 64 runs.

questions.prompt: Your PR has a merge conflict in `LoginPage.java`: main renamed a locator, your branch added a method. How should you resolve it?
options: Accept your version and drop main's change
Open the file, keep both the rename and your new method, make your method use the new locator name, then compile and run the affected tests before committing
Delete the file and recreate it
questions.explanation: Conflict resolution means combining both intents, then verifying with a build and tests. Choosing one side discards work; force-pushing main rewrites shared history.

coding.title: Simulate git bisect
coding.prompt:
Commits are listed oldest to newest. The first is known good and the last is known bad. Write `first_bad(commits, is_bad)` that finds the first bad commit with a binary search, calling `is_bad(commit)` as few times as possible. Return `(commit, calls)` where `calls` is how many times you called `is_bad`.

Assume once a commit is bad, all later ones are bad. Do not call `is_bad` on the first or last commit.

```python
first_bad(['a','b','c','d','e'], lambda c: c >= 'c')  # ('c', 2)
```
coding.explanation: The invariant is: commits[lo] is good and commits[hi] is bad. Each test halves the gap, so 64 commits need about 6 runs. When lo and hi are neighbours, hi is the first bad commit. That is exactly what git bisect does.
hints: Keep two indexes: lo (known good) and hi (known bad).
Test the middle; move hi there if it is bad, else move lo.
Stop when hi == lo + 1 and return commits[hi].

tests.name: finds the culprit
tests.code:
c, n = first_bad(['a','b','c','d','e'], lambda x: x >= 'c')
assert c == 'c', c

tests.name: logarithmic number of calls
tests.code:
commits = list(range(65))
c, n = first_bad(commits, lambda x: x >= 41)
assert c == 41 and n <= 6, (c, n)

tests.name: culprit right after good
tests.code:
c, n = first_bad(['g','x','y'], lambda v: v != 'g')
assert c == 'x', c
c, n = first_bad(['g','b'], lambda v: True)
assert (c, n) == ('b', 0), (c, n)

coding.title: Parse git status --porcelain
coding.prompt:
`git status --porcelain` prints two status characters, a space, then the path. The first character is the staging area (index), the second is the working tree. `??` means untracked.

Write `summarise(output)` returning a dict with sorted lists under keys `staged`, `unstaged` and `untracked`. A file can be in both staged and unstaged (e.g. `MM`).

```python
summarise('M  a.java\n M b.java\n?? c.txt\n')
# {'staged': ['a.java'], 'unstaged': ['b.java'], 'untracked': ['c.txt']}
```
coding.explanation: The porcelain format is stable for scripts: column 1 is the index, column 2 the working tree, and the path starts at column 4. Reading them separately is why 'MM' lands in both lists: part of the change is staged and more edits were made afterwards.
hints: Do not strip the line first: the leading space is meaningful.
x = line[0], y = line[1], path = line[3:].
'??' is untracked; otherwise a non-space x means staged and a non-space y means unstaged.

tests.name: basic three states
tests.code:
r = summarise('M  a.java
 M b.java
?? c.txt
')
assert r == {'staged':['a.java'],'unstaged':['b.java'],'untracked':['c.txt']}, r

tests.name: partly staged file in both
tests.code:
r = summarise('MM x.java\nA  new.java\n')
assert r == {'staged':['new.java','x.java'],'unstaged':['x.java'],'untracked':[]}, r

tests.name: deleted in working tree
tests.code:
r = summarise(' D old.java\n')
assert r['unstaged'] == ['old.java'] and r['staged'] == [], r
